html:
In 1924 the Soviet government redrew the map of Central Asia along national lines, creating the units that became today's Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan. The old units, the Turkestan republic and the people's republics of Bukhara and Khwarazm that had replaced the Uzbek khanates, were dissolved.

The policy, called national delimitation, gave each recognised nation its own territory, following the theory of nations shaped by Stalin. In October 1924 the Uzbek and Turkmen Soviet republics were created. Tajikistan began as an autonomous republic inside Uzbekistan and became a full republic in 1929; the Kazakh and Kyrgyz units became full republics in 1936.

Drawing lines through a mixed land of oases and nomads left many people outside "their" republic. Persian-speaking Samarkand and Bukhara went to Uzbekistan, and the Fergana Valley was split three ways, with enclaves inside enclaves. These lines became international borders when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, and they still cause disputes, such as clashes on the Kyrgyz and Tajik border. Jadid intellectuals like Fitrat helped give the new nations their languages and histories. See Russian and Soviet rule.
